translation:
_Gaam Sokhde saadh sabhi rahe, taki baat aay sabe kahe._ (In the village of Sokhda dwell all manner of holy men [sadhus]; everyone who comes tells their stories.)

In the village of Sokhda a number of sadhus used to live; everyone who came would tell their tales. In Sokhda there lived Jagaji, a disciple of Guru Gopaldasji (the guru of Jivanji Maharaj). His seat (hermitage) is in the forest. It is known today by the name of the "Valley Saint" (Veliya). If one wants to see what a real forest looks like, this place is like a magnificent forest. Nowadays, because of development, what was once wilderness has been turned into something pleasant and garden-like, but when I saw it before this development happened, in 1997, it looked like a fearsome forest. The followers of Jagaji are the native people of Sokhda. They have built a grand marble temple to Jagaji in Sokhda. Jagaji's followers use two hymns from Adhyaruji's compositions — the aarti and the vani. These followers of Jagaji state that his appearance (praagatya) was in [Samvat] 1117, but this is a mistake: Padmanabhji's appearance was in 1457 and Jivanji's appearance was in 1660, so Jagaji's appearance must have been around 1600. In a handwritten manuscript obtained from Kunvarpura village there are sakhis (couplets) of Jagaji, so it is likely that this Jagaji had some connection with the community of devotees (bhakt samaj). We shall therefore recognize this place of Sokhda as the seat of Jivanji's guru-brother (a fellow disciple of the same guru). Ritualism (karmakand) had a strong influence in Jagaji's tradition, so when Jivanji's devotees heard of the fame of Jagaji's saint, they went to meet him. Although Jivanji had forbidden it, they went anyway. But on hearing discussions that felt watery and unsatisfying, they began to regret it, and, realizing that Jivanji Maharaj had been right to forbid their going there, they were glad. Even though this village of Sokhda is the village of Jagaji's disciples, the Mahant Hariprasad of the Swaminarayan sect has had a grand ashram built there. Because of this, the people of the village have been drawn toward the Swaminarayan sect.
